title: Synchronisation and deadlock
subtitle: Two processes sharing one variable can corrupt it without either being wrong. Locks fix that — and create a new way to get stuck.

sections.title: The race condition
sections.body:
Suppose two processes both run counter++. That single line is really three machine steps: load the counter, add one, store it back. If the scheduler switches between the load and the store, both processes read the same old value and one increment is lost. The result depends on the exact interleaving — a race condition.

The stretch of code that touches shared data is the critical section. A correct solution needs mutual exclusion (one process inside at a time), progress (someone gets in if nobody is) and bounded waiting (nobody waits forever).

questions.prompt: Two processes each execute counter++ once, starting from 5. Which final values are possible without synchronisation?

choices.text: 6 or 7 — it depends on the interleaving.
Only 6, because the scheduler always switches at the worst moment.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Adding 1 twice is 7 only if the two updates cannot overlap. Without a lock they can, and then one of them is silently lost.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: If one process finishes its load-add-store before the other starts, the result is 7. If both load before either stores, both write 6. The program is not wrong in either run; it is non-deterministic, which is what makes races so hard to debug.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: The bad interleaving is possible, not guaranteed. A test may pass a million times and still fail in production.

figures.caption: Figure 3.1.1 — a lost update
figures.note: Two increments, final value 6 instead of 7: the second store overwrote the first.
figures.script:
diagram("mode: sequence
[Process A] as a
[counter in memory] as m
[Process B] as b
a -> m : load (reads 5)
b -> m : load (reads 5)
a -> a : add 1 → 6
b -> b : add 1 → 6
a -> m : store 6
b -> m : store 6
loop 6");

sections.title: Mutex, semaphore, monitor
sections.body:
A mutex is a lock with one owner: acquire before the critical section, release after. A semaphore is an integer with two atomic operations — wait (P) decrements and blocks if the result would be negative, signal (V) increments and wakes a waiter. Initialised to 1 it is a mutex; initialised to n it lets n processes in (a pool of identical resources). A monitor packages the data, the operations and the lock together so a caller cannot forget to lock.

Three classic exercises use them. Producer–consumer: a bounded buffer with semaphores empty = N, full = 0 and a mutex. Readers–writers: many readers or one writer. Dining philosophers: five forks on a table — if everyone grabs the left fork first, all wait forever.

questions.prompt: A semaphore is initialised to 0 and a process executes wait() on it. What happens?

choices.text: It blocks until some other process calls signal().
It continues immediately and the value becomes −1.
It raises an error, because a semaphore must start at 1.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: With value 0 there is nothing to take, so wait cannot decrement and the process sleeps on the semaphore’s queue. Initialising to 0 is how one process waits for an event another will announce.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: A negative value is only bookkeeping for the number of sleepers; the calling process is still put to sleep.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Any non-negative start is legal: 1 for a mutex, 0 for signalling, n for a resource pool.

figures.caption: Figure 3.2.1 — bounded buffer
figures.note: Two counting semaphores track free and used slots; the mutex protects the buffer itself.

sections.title: Deadlock and its four conditions
sections.body: A deadlock is a set of processes each waiting for something only another member of the set can release. It needs all four of these at once: mutual exclusion (resources are not shareable), hold and wait (keep what you have while asking for more), no pre-emption (resources cannot be taken away) and circular wait (a cycle of who-waits-for-whom). Break any one and deadlock is impossible — that is prevention. Avoidance allows all four but refuses any request that could lead to a stuck state; detection and recovery lets it happen and then kills or rolls back a victim; ignoring it (the ostrich approach) is what most general-purpose systems actually do.

questions.prompt: Which single condition does “lock the resources in a fixed global order” break?

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Processes still hold some resources while asking for others; only the order of asking is constrained.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: If every process acquires resources in increasing order, a cycle would need some process to ask for a lower-numbered resource while holding a higher one — which the rule forbids. The other three conditions still hold.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: The resources are still exclusive. Breaking mutual exclusion needs shareable resources, which a printer or a lock is not.

figures.caption: Figure 3.3.1 — resource-allocation cycle
figures.note: A cycle P1 → R2 → P2 → R1 → P1: circular wait. Neither can proceed.
figures.script:
diagram("direction: right
[P1 holds R1] as p1 #blue
[P2 holds R2] as p2 #violet
[R1] as r1 #amber
[R2] as r2 #amber
p1 -> r2 : wants
p2 -> r1 : wants
r1 --> p1 : held by
r2 --> p2 : held by
@0 p1 -> r2 : request
@1.2 p2 -> r1 : request
loop 4");

sections.title: The banker's algorithm
sections.body:
The banker treats each process's maximum claim like a credit line. A state is safe if there is some order in which every process can be given its remaining need and finish. The algorithm keeps a vector Work (initially Available) and repeatedly looks for a process whose Need = Max − Allocation fits inside Work; it runs that process to completion and adds its allocation back. If all processes can be retired, the state is safe and the order found is a safe sequence. An unsafe state is not a deadlock — it is a state from which deadlock can no longer be ruled out.

Run the classic example: 5 processes, 3 resource types, Available = (3 3 2).

worked.why: Need = Max − Allocation. For P1: Max (3 2 2) − Allocation (2 0 0) = (1 2 2). With Work = Available = (3 3 2), (1 2 2) ≤ (3 3 2), so P1 can finish.
P1 finishes and returns its allocation: Work = (3 3 2) + (2 0 0) = (5 3 2). Now P3 (Need (0 1 1)) fits.
Continuing this way retires the remaining processes one by one: the card gives P1 P3 P0 P2 P4. Every process could be finished, so the state is safe.

questions.prompt: A state is unsafe. What does that tell you?

choices.text: At least one process has exceeded its maximum claim.
Deadlock is now possible — the banker refuses to enter it.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: A deadlocked state is unsafe, but an unsafe state need not be deadlocked yet.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Exceeding the claim is an error the algorithm rejects outright; unsafe is about feasibility of finishing, not about cheating.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Unsafe means no order is guaranteed to let everyone finish; whether deadlock actually occurs depends on what the processes do next. Avoidance is conservative: it denies requests that lead to unsafe states even though some would have turned out fine.

figures.caption: Figure 3.4.1 — banker's algorithm
figures.note: The algorithm retires processes in the order P1 P3 P0 P2 P4; any safe sequence proves the state safe.

figures.caption: Figure 3.4.2 — a request
figures.note: P1 asks for (1 0 2). The banker pretends to grant it and re-runs the safety check.

problems.prompt: Five processes and three resource types with Available = (3 3 2); Max and Allocation as in Figure 3.4.1. Is the system in a safe state? Give a safe sequence.
problems.answer: Yes. The algorithm repeatedly picks the lowest-numbered unfinished process whose Need fits in Work. It finds P1 P3 P0 P2 P4. Other orders such as P1, P3, P4, P0, P2 are also safe — a safe state may have many safe sequences.

problems.prompt: Name the four Coffman conditions and say which one a spooling printer queue removes.
problems.answer: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no pre-emption, circular wait. Spooling removes mutual exclusion (for the printer): processes write to a queue on disk instead of holding the device, so they never wait on each other for it.

problems.prompt: Five philosophers each pick up their left fork first. Why can the table deadlock, and give one fix.
problems.answer: If all five pick up their left fork simultaneously, each holds one fork and waits for the right one held by a neighbour: circular wait. Fixes: allow at most four to sit at once, pick up both forks atomically (or neither), or number the forks and always take the lower one first.

sections.title: What to remember
sections.body:
• A race condition is a bug in the interleaving, not in any one process; a critical section guarded by a lock removes it.
  • Mutex = semaphore with value 1; semaphore 0 = signalling; semaphore n = pool.
  • Deadlock needs all four conditions; breaking one prevents it.
  • Safe ⇒ no deadlock guaranteed; unsafe ⇒ deadlock possible. The banker only ever grants requests that keep the state safe.

questions.prompt: Which statement about unsafe states is true?

choices.text: Unsafe and deadlocked mean the same thing.
A safe state can still deadlock if a process is unlucky.
Every deadlocked state is unsafe, but not every unsafe state is deadlocked.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Unsafe is a prediction about what might happen; deadlocked is a fact about what has.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: By definition a safe sequence exists, and following it finishes everyone.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Safe ⊂ not-deadlocked: no safe state leads to deadlock, but an unsafe state merely lacks the guarantee.
